body.statement: Under \(d^\star\), let \(b_{n,\varepsilon}=\mathbb P_{d^\star}(G_n(\varepsilon)^c)\). On \(G_n(\varepsilon)\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{\varepsilon}\mid F)=\sigma^2(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\), and \[\frac{\sigma^2}{n(1+\varepsilon)}\Sigma_k(d^\star)^{-1}\preceq\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{\varepsilon}\mid F)\preceq\frac{\sigma^2}{n(1-\varepsilon)}\Sigma_k(d^\star)^{-1}.\] Unconditionally, \[R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)=\sigma^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\left[\mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}\operatorname{tr}((F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1})\right]+\|\beta\|_2^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.\] Furthermore, \(b_{n,\varepsilon}\le\min\{1,\delta_{n,\varepsilon}\}\), where \(\delta_{n,\varepsilon}=2q\exp\{-n\varepsilon^2/(3\mu^\star)\}\), and \[\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}\frac{1-b_{n,\varepsilon}}{1+\varepsilon}\le R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)\le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1-\varepsilon)}+B^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.\] The upper bound also implies \[R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)\le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}(1+2\varepsilon)+2B^2q\exp\{-n\varepsilon^2/(3\mu^\star)\}.\]
body.proof_tex:
Write \(\Sigma=\Sigma_k(d^\star)\) and define the proof-intermediate whitened rows \(w_a=\Sigma^{-1/2}x_a\).  Since \(0<u\le1/2\), the vector \(d^\star\) lies in \((0,1)^p\), so the trace identity proves that \(\Sigma\) is positive definite and the whitening is well defined.  Product randomization across units and the definition of \(\Sigma\) give independence of \(w_1,\ldots,w_n\) and
\[
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}[w_aw_a^{\mathsf T}]
 =\Sigma^{-1/2}\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_ax_a^{\mathsf T}]\Sigma^{-1/2}
 =I_q.
\]
The exact-leverage proposition and the finite Boolean support imply, almost surely,
\[
 \lambda_{\max}(w_aw_a^{\mathsf T})
 =\|w_a\|_2^2
 =x_a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}x_a
 \le\mu^\star. \tag{1}
\]

Apply the cited matrix Chernoff theorem to \(K_a=w_aw_a^{\mathsf T}\).  These matrices are independent and positive semidefinite, (1) supplies \(R=\mu^\star>0\), and
\[
 \sum_{a=1}^n\mathbb E K_a=nI_q,
 \qquad \mu_{\min}=\mu_{\max}=n.
\]
For \(0\le t\le1/2\), put
\[
 h_+(t)=(1+t)\log(1+t)-t,
 \qquad
 h_-(t)=t+(1-t)\log(1-t).
\]
Both functions and their first derivatives vanish at zero, while
\[
 h_+''(t)=\frac{1}{1+t}\ge\frac23,
 \qquad
 h_-''(t)=\frac{1}{1-t}\ge1.
\]
Integrating twice from zero yields \(h_+(t)\ge t^2/3\) and \(h_-(t)\ge t^2/2\ge t^2/3\).  The two Chernoff bounds therefore give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb P\!\left\{\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{a=1}^nK_a\right)
 \le1-\varepsilon\right\}
 &\le q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\},\\
 \mathbb P\!\left\{\lambda_{\max}\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{a=1}^nK_a\right)
 \ge1+\varepsilon\right\}
 &\le q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\}.
\end{aligned} \tag{2}
\]
Now
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{a=1}^nK_a
 =\Sigma^{-1/2}(F^{\mathsf T}F/n)\Sigma^{-1/2}
 =I_q+H_n(\varepsilon).
\]
For a symmetric matrix, failure of \(\|H_n(\varepsilon)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon\) entails one of the two weak tail events in (2).  The union bound thus proves
\[
 b_{n,\varepsilon}
 \le2q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\}
 =\delta_{n,\varepsilon}.
\]
Together with the elementary probability bound \(b_{n,\varepsilon}\le1\), this is
\(b_{n,\varepsilon}\le\min\{1,\delta_{n,\varepsilon}\}\).

On \(G_n(\varepsilon)\), the definition of the operator norm and congruence by \(\Sigma^{1/2}\) give
\[
 (1-\varepsilon)\Sigma
 \preceq F^{\mathsf T}F/n
 \preceq(1+\varepsilon)\Sigma. \tag{3}
\]
Because \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) and \(\Sigma\) is positive definite, (3) makes \(F^{\mathsf T}F\) positive definite on this event.  Inversion reverses Loewner order, so
\[
 \frac{1}{n(1+\varepsilon)}\Sigma^{-1}
 \preceq(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}
 \preceq\frac{1}{n(1-\varepsilon)}\Sigma^{-1}. \tag{4}
\]
For every realization of \(F\) in \(G_n(\varepsilon)\), the linear-response assumption and the estimator definition yield
\[
 \widehat\beta_\varepsilon-\beta
 =(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}F^{\mathsf T}\epsilon.
\]
Conditional centering consequently gives zero conditional mean, and conditional homoskedasticity gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_\varepsilon\mid F)
 &=(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}F^{\mathsf T}
   (\sigma^2I_n)F(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\\
 &=\sigma^2(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}.
\end{aligned} \tag{5}
\]
Here \(\sigma>0\) follows from the stated variance range.  Multiplying (4) by \(\sigma^2\) proves the claimed conditional covariance sandwich.

The target coefficient remains distinct from its observed-law identifying functional.  Indeed, linear response, iterated expectation, and conditional centering show
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_aY_a]
 &=\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_ax_a^{\mathsf T}]\beta
   +\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_a\epsilon_a]\\
 &=\Sigma\beta
   +\mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[x_a\mathbb E(\epsilon_a\mid F)\right]
 =\Sigma\beta.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus invertibility established above proves, rather than defines, the relation
\(\beta=\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_aY_a]\).

The event \(G_n(\varepsilon)\) is measurable with respect to \(F\).  On that event, (5) and the zero conditional mean imply
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[\|\widehat\beta_\varepsilon-\beta\|_2^2\mid F\right]
 =\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}.
\]
On its complement, the estimator definition gives \(\widehat\beta_\varepsilon=0\), so the squared error is exactly \(\|\beta\|_2^2\).  Splitting over these two disjoint events and taking expectations proves the exact decomposition
\[
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 =\sigma^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[
   \mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}
   \operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}\right]
 +\|\beta\|_2^2b_{n,\varepsilon}. \tag{6}
\]
Taking traces in (4), using
\(\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1})=\Phi^\star\), multiplying by
\(\mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}\), and averaging gives
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1+\varepsilon)}(1-b_{n,\varepsilon})
 \le
 \sigma^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[
   \mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}
   \operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}\right]
 \le
 \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1-\varepsilon)}(1-b_{n,\varepsilon}).
\]
For the lower risk bound, add the nonnegative fallback term in (6).  For the upper risk bound, drop the factor \(1-b_{n,\varepsilon}\le1\) and use \(\|\beta\|_2^2\le B^2\).  This yields exactly
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}\frac{1-b_{n,\varepsilon}}{1+\varepsilon}
 \le R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 \le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1-\varepsilon)}+B^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.
\]
Finally, \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) implies
\[
 \frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}\le1+2\varepsilon,
\]
and the Chernoff bound gives
\(B^2b_{n,\varepsilon}\le2B^2q\exp\{-n\varepsilon^2/(3\mu^\star)\}\).  Substitution proves
\[
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 \le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}(1+2\varepsilon)
 +2B^2q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\}.
\]
Every step used only the stated first two conditional noise moments; no conditional Gaussianity or other noise-law condition is needed.
body.justification: The theorem verifies the exact Chernoff constant and keeps the fallback bias in the unconditional risk.
body.gap: Tropp2012 supplies the tail tool and HsuKakadeZhang2014 supplies general decompositions, but neither gives this product-Fourier leverage calibration or fallback branch.
body.consumer: The bound converts the exact population design into an auditable finite-sample precision guarantee.
